frozen_question: Does Dendera X, p.89,7-10 / pl.42 show the Mendes/Banebdjedet phallus-and-spine relic in a physical vessel whose morphology can be analyzed as a container, including opening, lid, cavity or insertion geometry?

method_execution.TOPA_SPIDER: Trace Banebdjedet + phallus/spine references through Cauville/Dendera X and later iconographic scholarship.
method_execution.FIVE_D_SPIRAL: text -> plate reference -> deity/location -> relic content -> vessel morphology -> material-function contradiction return
method_execution.BEETLE_GRAZER: Separate repeated citations to the same Dendera scene from independent visual witnesses.
method_execution.TENET_REVERSE: Work backward from modern claims of a Mendes reliquary to the exact Dendera scene and plate.
method_execution.visual_boundary: No cavity, lid, aperture or internal geometry is asserted until the primary plate or an equivalent high-resolution photograph is actually inspected.

textual_witness.source: Sylvie Cauville, Le temple de Dendara, Tome X, Osirian chapels, 1997
textual_witness.finding: In the Osirian canopic/relic procession, Banebdjedet/Mendes is associated with and brings the known Osirian relics of the backbone/spine and phallus.
textual_witness.procession_context: Scholarly discussion of the introductory procession wording states that the local relics are enclosed/carried in vessels.

iconography_witness.secondary_reproduction: Modern iconographic study identifies a ram-headed human-form Banebdjedet in the Dendera eastern Osirian chapel, citing Cauville 1997 p.89, pl.42.
iconography_witness.boundary: The secondary reproduction currently available does not resolve the vessel's interior engineering and cannot substitute for a primary high-resolution plate.

negative_controls: A deity shown ram-headed is not automatically a ram-headed reliquary.
A textual statement that relics are in vessels does not identify the exact vessel morphology in pl.42.
A later drawing or iconographic reconstruction cannot establish an opening/cavity that is invisible in the primary plate.
Mendes/Banebdjedet presence does not prove a surviving archaeological counterpart.

sources.title: Le temple de Dendara, Tome X

sources.use: Banebdjedet brings spine and phallus; procession language describes relics in vessels
Identifies ram-headed Banebdjedet in scene cited to Cauville pl.42
Confirms ongoing/new photographic documentation of the Osirian chapels and prior publication of Dendera X

canonical_seal: 𓊽 THE DENDERA TEXT PUTS MENDES' PHALLUS AND SPINE INTO A RELIC-VESSEL SYSTEM. THE EXACT SHAPE OF PLATE 42 IS NOT YET OURS TO INVENT. 𓊽
